confirmed: Source identity is correct: Is ChatGPT detrimental to innovation? A field experiment among university students, by Mazen Hassan, Engi Amin, Sarah Mansour and Zeyad Kelani; bioRxiv preprint doi:10.1101/2024.04.03.588037, version posted April 5, 2024. The supplied PDF has 32 pages, including appended main figures and tables; it is not the journal version implied by the filename (PDF p. 1 and its version notice; pp. 23-32).

The paper reports course-level randomization: existing enrollment in Social Network Analysis versus Data Mining defines the assignment unit, and the authors explicitly call it randomization. Retain field_rct and context_class=none for two-screener routing, with the existing caveat that the chance procedure is unspecified; individual randomization is not reported (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181; p. 17, Discussion, lines 371-377).

Social-science undergraduates at an Egyptian public university submitted three graded essays over one month in April 2023. Social Network Analysis students were instructed to use ChatGPT; Data Mining students were not allowed to use it. The lab assessment followed one week after all assignments were submitted; no AI assistance is described for that assessment (PDF p. 7, lines 154-155; p. 8, lines 169-181; p. 9, lines 187-191; p. 10, lines 204-223).

The lemonade task lasted seven rounds, with six decision parameters including an advertising message or slogan of at most 20 words. Four external annotators rated the messages and were unaware of the research question and experimental design; these are output-scored creativity outcomes (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 204-223).

Counts are correctly distinguished: 94 subjects initially recruited, one discarded for missing payout information, then two anomalous observations removed using the 1.5xIQR rule. Table 1 lists 43 control and 50 ChatGPT participants, total 93; Table 2 has 91 observations in each subject-level innovation model. This is not a study with fewer than 50 analyzed people; the initial count is not explicitly an assignment count, and final arm-specific counts are not supplied (PDF p. 11, lines 242-244; p. 12, lines 254-256; p. 29, Table 1; p. 30, Table 2).

The aggregate exploration reported string matches the source: ChatGPT -0.719** (0.326) in model (1), -0.604* (0.328) in model (2), and 91 observations in each. Table 2 says results are clustered by Subject ID and defines ** p<0.05 and * p<0.1; the text reports Mann Whitney U test, p-value = 0.037 (PDF p. 30, Table 2; p. 13, Results, lines 272-288; p. 24, Figure 2).

The paper defines aggregate innovativeness using the average subject-specific standard deviation of choices for sugar content, lemon concentration and price. Although its prose describes approximately 0.6 to 0.72 standard deviation points, it does not identify a between-participant standardizer for an SMD; the form appropriately preserves the printed regression coefficients without calculating one (PDF p. 13, lines 272-288; p. 30, Table 2).

The advertising-message reported string is accurate: 265 unique messages, four coders, and Mann Whitney U test, p-value > 0.05. The 265 are outputs, not participants or ratings; the test aggregation and a separate analyzed participant count are not specified. Methods state a 0-to-10 creativity scale, while Results state 1 to 10; Figure 3 has no exact numerical point labels or printed arm means/SDs (PDF p. 10, lines 218-223; p. 14, lines 295-301; p. 25, Figure 3).

The one-line finding matches the 91-person innovation regression and the nonsignificant advertising-message comparison; it does not invent standardized effects or message-rating arm means (PDF p. 30, Table 2; p. 14, lines 295-301).

The supporting experimental script/S1 and appendix II are referenced but absent from the supplied PDF and markdown; the appended pages contain main Figures 1-6 and Tables 1-4. No supplementary results were treated as verified (PDF p. 9, lines 196-198; p. 11, lines 238-239; p. 14, lines 300-301; pp. 23-32).
This is one intervention sample with several later tasks, not a synthesis; no pooled estimates or study-count extraction is applicable (PDF pp. 8-14, Methods and Results).
summary: The preprint reports course-level randomization of ChatGPT assistance and an innovation analysis of 91 students, warranting the two-screener pipeline despite an unspecified allocation procedure. The main statistics and source version are accurate, but preregistration is explicitly stated and the component innovation results are omitted.
